concepts.title: Perception of Surface Orientation from Lines
concepts.one_liner: The orientation of a surface and the camera can be perceived through the arrangement of lines and their vanishing points.
concepts.content: The orientation of a surface and the camera can be inferred from the subtle arrangement of lines in a drawing. For example, in a drawing of floor tiles, the lines converge toward vanishing points. If these vanishing points are located above the drawing, it is compatible with a horizon line for a horizontal surface. Conversely, if a vanishing point is located below the figure, it creates the impression of looking at a vertical wall from a high camera angle. The orientation of the horizon line—the line connecting the vanishing points—further distinguishes between horizontal and vertical perceptions.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how humans perceive 3D structure from 2D lines is crucial for computer vision. It allows algorithms to infer surface orientation and camera pose from simple geometric features.
concepts.recap_md: The position of vanishing points relative to the image helps determine if a surface is horizontal or vertical.

slots.motivation: Understanding how humans perceive 3D structure from 2D lines is crucial for computer vision. It allows algorithms to infer surface orientation and camera pose from simple geometric features.

concepts.title: Vanishing Point
concepts.one_liner: A vanishing point is a point in a drawing where parallel lines appear to intersect.
concepts.content: A vanishing point is defined as the point in which parallel lines intersect in a perspective drawing. The location of these points provides information about the orientation of surfaces and the camera. For instance, vanishing points located above a drawing are compatible with a horizon line, whereas a vanishing point below a figure can give the impression of looking at a vertical wall from an elevated camera position.
concepts.motivation_md: Vanishing points are fundamental to perspective projection. They allow for the reconstruction of 3D geometry from 2D images by identifying the directions of parallel lines in space.
concepts.recap_md: Parallel lines in the 3D world converge to a single vanishing point in a 2D projection.

slots.motivation: Vanishing points are fundamental to perspective projection. They allow for the reconstruction of 3D geometry from 2D images by identifying the directions of parallel lines in space.

concepts.title: Horizon Line
concepts.one_liner: The horizon line is the line that connects two or more vanishing points of a plane.
concepts.content: The horizon line of a plane is the line that connects its vanishing points. Its orientation—whether horizontal or vertical—provides a cue for the orientation of the surface being viewed. For example, a horizontal horizon line is typical for a ground plane, while a vertical horizon line might suggest a vertical wall viewed from a specific camera angle.
concepts.motivation_md: The horizon line serves as a reference for determining the "eye level" or camera height and the tilt of the camera relative to a surface.
concepts.recap_md: The horizon line is formed by connecting the vanishing points of a planar surface.

concepts.title: Motion Blur
concepts.one_liner: Motion blur occurs when a camera sensor collects light while moving, resulting in an average of translated copies of an image.
concepts.content: When taking a picture from a moving vehicle, images often appear blurry because the camera sensor collects light over a period of time while the car is in motion. The resulting picture is the average of several translated copies of the same image. Notably, the amount of blur is not uniform; objects that are far away may remain sharp, while nearby objects appear very blurry. This effect is determined by the car's speed, the exposure time, and the distance between the camera and the objects in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion blur is a common artifact in photography and video. Understanding its relationship to distance and speed allows for depth estimation and image restoration in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: Motion blur is the result of averaging translated images during a camera's exposure time.

concepts.title: Principle of Continuity
concepts.one_liner: The principle of continuity suggests that smooth, continuous line segments are perceived as belonging to a single object.
concepts.content: The principle of continuity, identified by Gestalt psychologists, states that if you see smooth, continuous line segments, you assume they lie on a single object. This is based on the idea that it would be a significant coincidence for two separate objects to align their contours perfectly. [FIGURE:2962e76f5808a7be | A schematic drawing of a horizontal straight line intersected by a continuous sinusoidal wave. The wave oscillates symmetrically above and below the line, completing approximately two and a half...] [FIGURE:d7efe27713f24942 | A sequence of five parabolic shapes alternating between facing up and facing down, arranged along a horizontal axis. The shapes are disconnected, with three upward-facing arches on top and two...] While this principle usually holds, photographs often contain "accidents" or coincidences where contours from different objects align, such as a finger boundary aligning with a lip contour or creases on two different shirts appearing continuous.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle helps the visual system group features into coherent objects. In computer vision, it provides a heuristic for edge linking and object segmentation.
concepts.recap_md: Humans tend to group continuous, smooth lines as part of the same object.

concepts.title: Accidental Alignments and Coincidences
concepts.one_liner: Accidental alignments are coincidences in photographs where contours of separate objects perfectly align, potentially misleading vision algorithms.
concepts.content: In complex photographs containing thousands of tiny images, coincidences or "accidents" frequently occur where the contours of two different objects perfectly align. Generically, the principle of continuity suggests that smooth, continuous line segments belong to a single object, but these accidental alignments violate that rule. Examples include a finger boundary aligning with a lip contour or a sleeve boundary being tangent to a line on a different shirt. Vision algorithms must be designed to handle these exceptions, as assuming that no accidents occur can lead to errors in scene interpretation.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that "accidents" happen prevents vision systems from making false assumptions about object boundaries based solely on line continuity.
concepts.recap_md: Accidental alignments occur when unrelated object contours line up by chance from a specific viewpoint.

concepts.title: Cues for Support
concepts.one_liner: Cues for support, such as drop shadows and slack strings, help determine the physical relationship between objects and surfaces.
concepts.content: Determining whether one object supports another can be inferred from specific visual cues. A drop shadow provides a strong indication that an object, such as a ball, is positioned above a surface. Conversely, a slack string can provide evidence that an object is resting directly on the surface. The relative location between an object and its shadow on the ground is a powerful cue for establishing contact or distance.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding support relationships is essential for scene understanding and robotics, allowing a system to determine which objects are stable and how they interact physically.
concepts.recap_md: Drop shadows indicate the distance between an object and the surface below it.

concepts.title: Light Field Cameras
concepts.one_liner: Light field cameras use arrays of tiny lenses to capture a scene from hundreds of different viewing angles simultaneously.
concepts.content: Light field cameras are specially designed devices that capture what a scene looks like from hundreds of different viewing angles. This is achieved using an array of tiny lenses, similar to how individual raindrops on a window can each refract a panorama of the surrounding scene. By collecting light from multiple perspectives at once, these cameras provide a much richer data set than a standard single-view photograph.
concepts.motivation_md: Light field cameras allow for post-capture adjustments like refocusing and perspective shifts, providing more information about the 3D structure of a scene than traditional cameras.
concepts.recap_md: Light field cameras use lens arrays to capture multiple viewpoints of a scene in a single exposure.

concepts.title: Synthetic Refocusing
concepts.one_liner: Synthetic refocusing is the technique of adjusting an image's focus after capture by using high-density information to triangulate the depth of objects in a scene.
concepts.content: From a high density of information, vision systems can achieve many interesting tricks, such as triangulating the depth of objects in the scene and synthetically refocusing the image after it has been taken.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for post-capture adjustments to an image's focal point, providing flexibility in photography and depth analysis that traditional single-shot cameras cannot achieve.
concepts.recap_md: - It allows the focus of an image to be changed after the photo has been taken. - It relies on high-density information to triangulate the depth of objects within a scene.

concepts.title: Plato's Cave Allegory in Computer Vision
concepts.one_liner: Plato's Allegory of the Cave illustrates how images are crude 2D projections that collapse 3D geometry and occlude much of the underlying physical reality.
concepts.content: In the Allegory of the Cave, Plato imagined a group of prisoners chained up in a cave whose only experience of the outside world is through shadows cast on the cave's wall. When we look at images, we think we are directly seeing reality, but the situation is actually much more like Plato's cave. An image is a crude projection of the underlying physical state, collapsing 3D geometry into a flat 2D grid of pixels. From any given viewing angle, most of the scene is occluded, and materials are depicted only in terms of how photons bounce off their surfaces. One job of a vision system is to infer everything you cannot see given everything you can. The allegory also involves layers of indirection: the shadows are cast by puppets controlled by puppeteers who act out interpretations of the broader reality outside.
concepts.motivation_md: This allegory helps researchers understand the fundamental challenge of computer vision: reconstructing a complex, multi-dimensional reality from limited, flattened, and occluded 2D data.
concepts.recap_md: - Images are 2D projections that collapse 3D geometry and occlude much of the physical scene. - Vision systems must infer the underlying physical state from these incomplete shadows of reality.

concepts.title: Material Recognition

position.section_title: How Do You Know Something Is Wet?

concepts.one_liner: Material recognition is the visual ability to identify physical properties like wetness, temperature, and texture without direct physical contact.
concepts.content: Our visual system allows us to recognize not just objects, but also materials. We can tell if something will feel hot or cold, soft or hard, smooth or rugged. We can also recognize if something is wet or not without touching it, as seen with wet sand. This raises questions about why sand looks darker when wet, whether everything wet looks darker than when dry, and how we distinguish darkness caused by wetness from darkness caused by shadows. ![Why does wet sand look dark? The answer to this question is interesting, but not as much as the question itself.](figures/visionscience/wet_sand_2.jpeg){#fig-wet_sand width="80%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing materials is crucial for understanding how to interact with the environment, such as predicting tactile sensations or physical properties like temperature and friction from a distance.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual systems can infer tactile properties like hardness, temperature, and texture from images. - A key challenge is distinguishing material changes, like wetness, from lighting effects like shadows.

concepts.title: Pixel Recognition and Context
concepts.one_liner: The recognition of individual pixels depends on the context of the whole image rather than just local intensity.
concepts.content: Before building systems that can see, it is useful to look at images and pay attention to individual pixels. Even in a tiny $32 \times 32$ pixel image, we can often recognize content despite the low resolution. For example, a single dark gray pixel surrounded by white pixels might be identified as a pen, even if the pen is only three pixels long. Recognition of the meaning of that pixel cannot come just from the intensity of that pixel or the few pixels nearby, as many different objects could map to similar intensities. Instead, it is the whole image and the context that provides the necessary information. Taken in isolation, such pixels are impossible to recognize.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights that vision is not just a bottom-up process of identifying colors. It demonstrates the necessity of global context in resolving local ambiguities in low-resolution data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Individual pixel intensities are often insufficient for object recognition.
 - Global context allows the brain to assign meaning to ambiguous local features.
 - Recognizable images can be formed with surprisingly few pixels if context is preserved.

concepts.title: Vision as a Dynamical System

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Vision is a dynamical system where the longer one looks at an image, the more details and understanding are extracted.
concepts.content:
Visual perception cannot be formulated as a simple input-output function over predefined domains. Vision is a dynamical system, even when looking at a static image. The longer you look at an image, the more details you see and the better you understand the scene.

(see figure: A street in Paris. Is everything fine in this picture?)

However, this feeling of unlimited and effortless understanding is often an illusion. We may not truly understand everything we see; for example, in a manipulated image of a street in Paris, some chair legs might not correspond to any actual chair, challenging our initial perception of the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: To understand that vision is an active, temporal process rather than a single snapshot. It explains why we miss details initially and how our brain 'fills in' gaps that might not actually make sense.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vision is an active process that evolves over time even for static images.
 - Increased observation time leads to the extraction of finer scene details.
 - Perception can be illusory, masking inconsistencies in a scene through a sense of effortless understanding.

concepts.title: Visual Cognitive Load

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: Visual cognitive load refers to the increased likelihood of making judgment mistakes as the complexity of a visual task grows.
concepts.content: When solving a task, as the **visual cognitive load** increases, we are more likely to make judgment mistakes.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the limits of human visual processing is crucial for designing interfaces and safety systems where information overload can lead to critical errors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Higher visual cognitive load correlates with an increase in judgment errors.
 - It represents the mental effort required to process visual information for a specific task.

concepts.title: Image Patches as a Dataset

position.section_title: The More You Look, the More You See

concepts.one_liner: A single large image can be treated as a dataset by dividing it into thousands of tiny image patches.
concepts.content: Each patch within a larger image is essentially a small photo in its own right. Consequently, a single large image contains thousands of tiny images within it. This allows a single photo to be treated as *big data*; by chopping up the photo, you create a large dataset of tiny images. A common trick in computer vision is to take a method developed for processing a dataset and apply it to the set of patches in an image, or vice versa.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows researchers to apply statistical learning methods to single images, which is useful for tasks like texture synthesis, super-resolution, or training models when data is scarce.
concepts.recap_md:
- Large images can be decomposed into a dataset of smaller image patches.
 - Enables the application of dataset-oriented algorithms to individual images.
 - Treats local image regions as independent samples for analysis.

concepts.title: Learning to See Through Painting
concepts.one_liner: Learning to paint helps one understand the world by focusing on why objects look a certain way rather than just what they represent.
concepts.content: Learning to paint is an effective way of learning to see. Starting from a blank canvas and a finite set of paints, the goal is to replicate shadows, 3D shapes, and reflections to make an object look real. Artists learn to see the world not just by what it represents, but by why it looks the way it does. In the process of painting, such as a strawberry, realism may not increase monotonically; certain strokes might initially look less realistic but eventually provide the shading necessary to make the object appear three-dimensional.
concepts.motivation_md: By attempting to reconstruct an image from scratch, one gains a deeper appreciation for the physics of light, shading, and geometry that the visual system usually processes subconsciously.
concepts.recap_md:
- Painting requires understanding the 'why' of appearance (light, shadow, shape).
 - Realism in a visual representation may decrease temporarily to build necessary depth cues.
 - The process of artistic creation mirrors the decomposition of visual scenes into constituent elements.

concepts.title: Natural Pinhole Cameras in Tree Shadows
concepts.one_liner: Small gaps between tree leaves act as natural pinhole cameras, projecting images of the sun onto the ground.
concepts.content: Under the shadow of a tree on a sunny day, light rays passing through holes between leaves create spots on the floor. While one might expect these spots to have irregular shapes matching the gaps, they are actually circular and of similar size. This occurs because the gaps act as **pinhole cameras**. When the openings are small enough, the shape of the projected light is dominated by the shape of the light source—the sun—rather than the shape of the opening. This effect is most clearly observed during a solar eclipse, where the tree's shadow contains many crescent-shaped images of the eclipsed sun.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the fundamental principles of image formation and the pinhole camera model using a common natural phenomenon, illustrating how light travels and projects images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gaps between leaves function as natural pinhole apertures.
 - The shape of the projected light spot reflects the shape of the light source (the sun).
 - During an eclipse, these natural pinholes project crescent shapes instead of circles.
